newsitem.title: USA: Democrats propose crime bill that targets gangs.
newsitem.headline: Democrats propose crime bill that targets gangs.

text.p: Senate Democrats Wednesday proposed legislation to fight gangs and violent juvenile criminals as the next step in the war against crime.

"Our bill targets youthful offenders for certain pounishment when they commit violent acts and helpful treatment when they need it," Vermont Sen. Patrick Leahy, the senior Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said at a news conference.
"The target should be youth violence and drugs. This bill provides swift and certain punishment," Sen. Joseph Biden of Delaware added.

They said their bill builds on the success of the 1994 crime bill, passed when Democrats last controlled Congress. That bill authorised funds to hire 100,000 local police, banned 19 types of semiautomatic weapons and increased federal penalties for several crimes.
"Since the 1994 crime law, violent crime is down and down significantly," Biden said.
"I am concerned that while the nation's overall crime rate is down, the juvenile crime rate is skyrocketing," Sen. John Breaux of Louisiana said.

The Democratic bill would increase federal penalties for the use of gang paraphernalia, such as body armour and laser sighting devices, and for threatening or using violence against witnesses, allow juveniles to be kept in jail until they are 26 instead of the current madatory release at age 21 and streamline procedures for trying juveniles as adults.
The $13 billion bill would also provide funds to build more prisons for juvenile criminals and for drug prevention and treatment programmes.

The bill will be introduced next week when Congress reconvenes after President Clinton's second inauguration on Monday. Majority Republicans are expected to introduce their own anti-crime legislation and Leahy and Biden said they hoped a bipartisan bill could be passed.
"We bring to the table the strong support of President Clinton," Leahy said.
Biden said he believed Judiciary Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican, will support much of the bill. He said most law enforcement officials endorsed the bill.
Crime bills have been one of the most partisan issues in Congress in recent years, with each party trying to show it is tougher than the other against criminals.
